title: Git Isn't a Diff Tracker: How Blobs, Trees, DAG Commits, and the Index Actually Work Under the Hood
summary:
S M Tahosin Posted on Oct 10 Git Isn't a Diff Tracker: How Blobs, Trees, DAG Commits, and the Index Actually Work Under the Hood # git # programming # devops # webdev Ask most developers how Git works, and you will hear a familiar explanation: "Git tracks changes. When you edit a file and commit, Git calculates the diff between the old file and the new file and saves the patch." It is a completely reasonable mental model. After all, when you run git diff or git show , the terminal prints green additions and red deletions. Older version control systems like CVS and Subversion (SVN) worked exactly that way: they stored a base file and appended delta patches across time. There is only one problem: Git does not work that way at all. Git does not track file diffs. Git does not store patches. Git does not even have an internal concept of "file renames". Underneath its porcelain command line interface, Git is something radically simpler and far more elegant: an immutable, content-addressed key-value object store sitting underneath a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of snapshot trees. When developers treat Git as a magical incantation machine, commands like git rebase , git reset --mixed , or a detached HEAD state feel like minefields. But the moment you look inside the .git folder and understand how Git represents data, the mystery dissolves. Here is what actually happens under the hood when you use Git. 1. Peeking Inside .git : The Content-Addressed Object Store When you type git init in an empty folder, Git does not set up a server or connect to a daemon. It creates a single hidden directory named .git . Inside that directory, the most important folder is .git/objects . This folder is Git's database. Every piece of data in your project, every file, every directory listing, every commit message, and every tag, is stored here as one of four fundamental object types : Blob : Stores raw file contents (uncompressed byte streams). It does not store file names, paths, or file permissions. Tree : Represents a directory. It maps file names and file permissions to the cryptographic hashes of blobs and child trees. Commit : A snapshot pointer. It references a top-level root tree, zero or more parent commit hashes, an author, a committer, and a commit message. Annotated Tag : A permanent pointer to a specific commit, containing a tagger name, date, and verification message. The Cryptographic Hash (Content-Addressing) Git identifies every object by its cryptographic hash. In standard Git, this is a 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 string (newer versions can also use SHA-256). Let us demonstrate this with raw plumbing commands. If you create a file with the content hello world\n and pass it to Git's low-level hash calculation tool: $ echo "hello world" | git hash-object -w --stdin 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The -w flag instructs Git to write the object directly into .git/objects . How did Git compute 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad ? Git prepends a standardized header to the raw data: the object type ( blob ), a space, the content length in bytes, and a null byte ( \0 ). Then it passes the concatenated buffer through the SHA algorithm: header  = "blob 12\0"
content = "hello world\n"
store   = header + content

sha1("blob 12\0hello world\n") = 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Notice what is missing from this calculation: the file name . If you name that file README.md , main.py , or config.json , the SHA hash is identical. If five different directories in your project contain an identical file, Git stores that blob exactly once . How Git Organizes the File System Inspect .git/objects after writing that blob, and you will see: .git/objects/
├── 3b/
│   └── 18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Git takes the first two characters of the 40-character hash ( 3b ) and creates a subfolder. The remaining 38 characters become the filename. This split prevents operating systems from choking when thousands of objects accumulate in a single directory. The file on disk is compressed using zlib. You can inspect its contents and type at any time using Git's inspection tool, git cat-file : # Check the object type $ git cat-file -t 3b18e512
blob # Print the uncompressed contents $ git cat-file -p 3b18e512
hello world Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 2. The Snapshot Architecture: Why Git Never Stores Diffs Because older version control tools stored delta diffs, many developers assume Git calculates differences when saving new commits. In reality, Git stores complete snapshots . When you commit a change, Git creates a new Tree object representing your root folder. That Tree object contains a complete manifest of every file and folder in the project. The Efficiency of Immutable Trees You might wonder: If Git stores full snapshots rather than diffs, why doesn't my repository size explode into gigabytes after twenty commits? The secret is content-addressable structural sharing . Suppose your repository contains 1,000 files across 20 folders. You open docs/guide.md , fix a single typo, and run git commit . Here is what Git does: It hashes the new docs/guide.md and writes one new blob into .git/objects . It creates a new Tree object for the docs/ folder. This tree points to the new blob for guide.md , but reuses the existing hashes for all unchanged files in docs/ . It creates a new root Tree object. This root tree points to the new docs/ tree, but reuses the exact same hashes for the other 19 unchanged folder trees. It creates a new Commit object pointing to the new root tree. 999 files were not copied or re-hashed. Their pointers remained identical across the tree hierarchy. Because blobs and trees are immutable, Git reuses them indefinitely. If a 100MB asset never changes across 500 commits, it takes up 100MB of disk space, not 50GB. When Does Git Actually Use Deltas? (Packfiles) Git does use delta compression, but only during optimization , never during normal commit creation. As you work, loose objects accumulate in .git/objects . Periodically, or when you run git gc (garbage collection) or git push , Git packs loose objects into a Packfile ( .pack ) alongside an index file ( .idx ). Inside a packfile, Git runs an intelligent sliding-window delta compression algorithm. It compares files with similar sizes and paths, identifies common patterns, and stores one file as a full version and the others as reverse deltas. This two-tier architecture gives Git the best of both worlds: O(1) instantaneous snapshot creation during development, and minimal network transfer during pushes and pulls. 3. The Three Trees: Working Directory, Index, and HEAD To understand how commands like add , commit , checkout , and reset actually work, you must visualize Git as managing three separate trees . 1. The Working Directory (Filesystem) This is the physical sandbox on your hard drive where you edit files in your editor. These are regular, uncompressed files that your operating system and tools interact with directly. 2. The Index (The Staging Area) The index is not an abstract concept; it is a physical binary file located at .git/index . The index is a cache that pre-computes what your next commit will look like. When you execute git add path/to/file : Git reads the file from your working directory. It writes a new compressed blob into .git/objects . It records the file path, permissions, and the new blob's SHA hash inside .git/index . The staging area is effectively an in-memory draft of a Tree object, waiting to be sealed into a commit. 3. The HEAD (Last Committed State) HEAD is a reference pointer. It tracks your current location in the repository's commit graph. Most of the time, HEAD points to a branch name, which in turn points to the most recent commit object in that branch. Demystifying git reset : The Three-Tree Slider Once you understand the three trees, Git's most feared command, git reset , becomes completely intuitive. git reset <commit-hash> is simply a slider that allows you to choose how many of the three trees to roll backward: git reset --soft HEAD~1 : Moves only HEAD backward by one commit. Your Index and Working Directory remain untouched. All changes from that commit remain staged, ready to be recommitted. git reset --mixed HEAD~1 (the default): Moves HEAD and updates the Index to match that previous commit. Your Working Directory remains untouched. Your changes are safe on disk, but appear as unstaged modifications. git reset --hard HEAD~1 : Moves HEAD , overwrites the Index , and overwrites your Working Directory . Any uncommitted changes on disk are permanently discarded. Instead of memorizing confusing command-line flags, visualize moving a pointer across the three tiers. 4. Branches and Merging: Pointers in a Directed Acyclic Graph In many traditional version control systems, creating a branch was an expensive operation: it copied the entire project directory tree into a separate /branches/feature folder. In Git, a branch is not a copy of your files. A branch is just a 41-byte text file. The Anatomy of a Branch Reference Look inside .git/refs/heads/ : $ ls .git/refs/heads/
main
feature-login Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Open .git/refs/heads/main in a text editor: 7c841a0293dbfc9d6138fbd8f11075677e4e892c Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode It is a single 40-character hex string followed by a newline character. When you create a new branch with git branch feature-auth , Git does not duplicate a single line of source code. It creates a new 41-byte text file named feature-auth containing the exact commit SHA that your current branch points to. This is why branch creation in Git takes less than one millisecond, regardless of whether your project contains ten files or ten million files. What is HEAD ? If branches are just pointers to commit objects, how does Git know which branch you are currently working on? Inspect .git/HEAD : $ cat .git/HEAD
ref: refs/heads/main Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode HEAD is a symbolic pointer that references your current branch file. When you run git commit : Git writes the new tree and commit object. The new commit points to the old commit as its parent. Git updates .git/refs/heads/main to point to the new commit's hash. HEAD does not move; it still points to main , which now points to the new commit. What is a "Detached HEAD"? When you run git checkout <commit-hash> instead of git checkout <branch-name> , Git writes the raw commit hash directly into .git/HEAD : $ cat .git/HEAD
7c841a0293dbfc9d6138fbd8f11075677e4e892c Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode You are now in a Detached HEAD state. It sounds intimidating, but it simply means: HEAD is pointing directly to a commit object rather than to a branch pointer. If you make commits in this state, the new commits are created normally, but no branch reference advances with them. If you switch branches, those commits become unreachable by name, which leads us to merging and rebasing. Merges: Fast-Forward vs Three-Way Merges When you merge branch B into branch A , Git evaluates the commit graph: Fast-Forward Merge : If branch A has not received any new commits since branch B branched off, Git does not create a merge commit. It simply moves the pointer in .git/refs/heads/A forward to match branch B . Three-Way Merge : If both branches have diverged with independent commits, Git must perform a 3-way merge. It identifies three distinct snapshots: The tip of Branch A (Ours). The tip of Branch B (Theirs). The Best Common Ancestor (the point where the two branches diverged). By comparing both tips against the common ancestor, Git determines which changes were made on which branch. It constructs a new Tree combining both sets of edits and writes a Merge Commit containing two parent hashes . 5. Rebase, Cherry-Pick, and the Safety Net of the Reflog Few topics generate as much confusion as the difference between git merge and git rebase . Both commands integrate changes from one branch into another, but they do it in fundamentally different ways in the commit graph. How git rebase Actually Works When you run: $ git checkout feature $ git rebase main Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Git does not modify your existing commits. Remember: Git objects are cryptographically immutable . If you change a commit's parent, its SHA hash changes completely. Instead, Git performs the following sequence: It identifies all commits unique to feature since it diverged from main . It temporarily saves the diffs of those commits into memory. It resets the feature branch pointer to point directly to the current tip of main . It replays each saved change onto the new base one by one, generating brand-new commit objects with brand-new SHA hashes. The original commits are left behind in the object database as orphaned nodes. Rebasing creates a clean, linear project history, but it rewrites commit history. This is why the universal golden rule of Git exists: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared public branch. The Ultimate Safety Net: The Reflog Suppose you accidentally ran a disastrous command: $ git reset --hard HEAD~5 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Five valuable commits appear to have vanished. Your working directory is reverted. git log shows no trace of your work. Do not panic. Git almost never deletes committed data immediately. Every time HEAD or a branch pointer moves in your local repository, Git logs the previous position in .git/logs/HEAD . This log is called the Reflog (Reference Log). Run: $ git reflog Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode You will see a chronological record of every pointer movement: 7c841a0 (HEAD -> main) HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~5
9e4b102 HEAD@{1}: commit: Implement user authentication
2a8f331 HEAD@{2}: commit: Add database connection pool Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The commits were never destroyed; only the pointer was moved. To recover your "lost" commits instantly, simply point a branch back to the commit hash recorded in the reflog: $ git branch recovery-branch 9e4b102 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Your five commits, along with all their trees and blobs, are restored immediately. Git keeps unreachable objects in .git/objects for at least 30 to 90 days before running automatic garbage collection ( git prune ). As long as you committed your work at least once, it is virtually impossible to permanently lose it. 6. Three Common Git Traps (And the Internal Fixes) Understanding Git's internal architecture immediately provides solutions to the three most frustrating problems developers encounter: Trap 1: Accidentally Committing a Large File or Secret A developer accidentally commits a 200MB database dump or an API key file, realizes the mistake, runs git rm data.sql , and commits again. The repository size remains 200MB, and the file is still visible in history. Why it happens: Running git rm only removes the file from future Tree objects. The previous Commit object still references the original Tree, which still points to the 200MB blob in .git/objects . The fix: To completely remove an object from history, you must rewrite the commit DAG using tools like git-filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner, and then force garbage collection: # Modern replacement for git filter-branch git-filter-repo --invert-paths --path data.sql
git reflog expire --expire = now --all git gc --prune = now --aggressive Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Trap 2: Merge Conflict Panic Developers often panic during merge conflicts because they look only at the conflict markers: <<<<<<< HEAD
const API_URL = "https://api.v1.prod.com";
=======
const API_URL = "https://api.v2.internal.net";
>>>>>>> feature-branch Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Why it happens: A conflict occurs because both branches modified the exact same lines of code relative to their common ancestor snapshot. The internal fix: Use Git's 3-way merge diff style to inspect what the ancestor originally had: git config --global merge.conflictstyle zdiff3 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Now conflict markers display the base version between the two branches: <<<<<<< HEAD
const API_URL = "https://api.v1.prod.com";
||||||| base
const API_URL = "http://localhost:3000";
=======
const API_URL = "https://api.v2.internal.net";
>>>>>>> feature-branch Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Seeing the common ancestor makes resolving the conflict straightforward: you immediately see what each side was trying to achieve. Trap 3: Blind Force Pushing ( git push --force ) When a developer rebases locally, pushing to remote fails because the remote branch's history has diverged. The common instinct is to run git push --force . Why it happens: --force overwrites the remote ref pointer unconditionally, potentially obliterating commits that a teammate pushed while you were rebasing. The internal fix: Always use --force-with-lease : git push --force-with-lease Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode This flag checks the remote ref before overwriting. If another developer pushed commits to that branch in the meantime, the push will abort, protecting their work while letting you rebase cleanly. The Mental Shift The difference between struggling with Git and mastering it comes down to a shift in perception: Stop thinking of Git as an opaque command-line tool that saves edits and file diffs. Git is a simple, elegant content-addressed database. Files are Blobs , addressed by their cryptographic hash. Folders are Trees , mapping names to hashes. Snapshots are Commits , pointing to trees and parents in a Directed Acyclic Graph. Branches and tags are just lightweight 41-byte text pointers . Merges and rebases are operations that navigate and reshape the graph. Once you visualize the underlying graph, confusing commands become predictable, broken branches are easily untangled, and the fear of losing code disappears completely. How did understanding Git internals change the way you navigate daily workflows? Have you ever had to rescue a production branch using the reflog, or untangle a complex rebase conflict using plumbing commands? title: Every Software Developer Has Blamed…
summary:
Sylwia Laskowska Posted on Oct 8 Every Software Developer Has Blamed… # discuss Relatable tech humor and shared grievances I got back from FrontKon in Prague today (well, technically yesterday, since I'm publishing this tomorrow), and I'm DEAD! 😂 The conference itself was fantastic, of course. Both my panel discussion and my talk went really well, and the Czech developer community is starting to feel like family. Greetings from your favorite senior software vývojářka ! 😀 I'll write my usual, more technical article next week. I want to approach the topic from a slightly different angle, so I need a bit more time for research. Meanwhile, flights from Gdańsk to Prague depart at the absolutely murderous hour of 6 AM, which means that at 3:30 AM today, I was still in Prague! And since some of you have recently been asking for another installment of my "You're a Real Software Developer Only If…" series, here you go! Who or what has every software developer blamed at least once? Here's my list! 1. Another Developer Obviously, if the code is terrible, it's never our fault. Someone else must have messed it up. A colleague from our team, someone from another team, or the developer who worked on the project before us. Quite often, though, that "other developer" turns out to be ourselves from six months ago. 😅 2. The Company Because the processes are terrible, the standards are nonexistent, and management clearly has no idea what they're doing. The poor developer has been thrown into this corporate machine and is now forced to fight an endless battle against the system. Things get a little awkward when you're self-employed and your company consists of… well, you. xD 3. Legacy Code The application could be just six months old, and somehow there will already be legacy code somewhere. And naturally, that legacy code is responsible for every bug, every delay, and every missed delivery deadline! 4. The Framework It's buggy! It's unpredictable! It's missing half the features we need! If I wrote my own framework, now THAT would be something! And why haven't I done it yet? Well, I never promised anyone I would! 😅 5. The Client Let's be real: our jobs would be so much easier and more enjoyable if it weren't for that annoying client who keeps asking for things and complaining about everything. 🤣 6. The Backend This is personally my first suspect whenever something goes wrong. If something doesn't work, it MUST be the fault of whoever wrote the backend. I mean, come on. Are you seriously suggesting that something could possibly be wrong with MY code??? 7. The Frontend And this is exactly what backend developers think about the frontend whenever someone reports a bug. Yes, yes, I know. In the age of AI, many of us have become full-stack developers, whether we wanted to or not. But deep down, our hearts will always belong a little more to one of those "ends." ☺️ 8. The Requirements Obviously. They're either too vague, poorly written, or based on some completely ridiculous idea invented by the stakeholders. And even if the requirements are absolutely perfect, there's probably something missing from the documentation anyway. 😉 9. The Cache Come on, admit it. If you've never told someone to "clear your cache," can you even call yourself a software developer??? 10. CORS Often the first suspect for junior developers whenever some mysterious error appears. Never mind that everything was working perfectly fine yesterday. It's probably CORS! 11. The Browser An obvious one. I mean, is it OUR fault that people still insist on using Safari??? 12. …And Eventually, Themselves Now, let's get a bit more serious for just a moment. There are two kinds of complaining. The first is just harmless grumbling, the same way we complain about bad weather. It's particularly popular in countries like Poland, where complaining is practically a form of small talk. But there's another kind. Of course, I'm not talking about situations where a project or the people you work with are genuinely toxic. Those situations absolutely exist, and sometimes you really do need to sit down and think about what to do next. But in other cases? Sometimes it's worth stopping for a moment and asking ourselves where WE fit into this picture of everything and everyone we're blaming. There's actually a well-known psychological phenomenon called the fundamental attribution error . In simple terms, it describes our tendency to overestimate someone's personality or character and underestimate their circumstances when explaining their behavior. There's also a closely related concept called the actor–observer bias , which describes a tendency to explain our own behavior in terms of circumstances while explaining other people's behavior in terms of their personal characteristics. And that's particularly interesting here. Think about what happens when WE mess something up: our code isn't exactly a masterpiece or we missed a deadline. We can usually come up with perfectly reasonable explanations. And often, those explanations are completely valid! Maybe we were feeling a little sick, so our productivity dropped. Maybe the plumber wouldn't stop talking, and we lost half the morning. Maybe the library documentation was terrible. A million things could have happened. But what happens when ANOTHER developer messes something up? What do we think? Unfortunately, quite often, it's simply: "What an idiot." But here's the thing. That other developer has a life, too. They have their own problems, crying children, plumbers who show up late, and a thousand other things going on that we know absolutely nothing about. We don't have access to their thoughts or their circumstances. So our brains take a shortcut. And suddenly, instead of thinking "maybe something happened," we decide that the person is simply incompetent. And that's the thought I'd like to leave you with today. I was going to add some profound, philosophical conclusion here, but everything I came up with sounded suspiciously like something written by Sylwia Coelho. So let's keep it simple. Let's just try to be a little more understanding toward one another. ❤️ And next time you find yourself blaming another developer, remember: somewhere out there, another developer is probably blaming you. 😂 If you enjoy my content, you can also follow me on LinkedIn . I’ve seen incidents where the backend gets blamed because latency suddenly jumps, while the actual trigger is a retry storm on the client side. A backend starts missing its deadline, the frontend retries, those retries increase backend load, latency gets worse, and suddenly the component that looks like the “cause” is actually one part of a feedback loop. If you follow one request across the client, gateway, service, cache, and database, the original fault and the component amplifying it can be two completely different things. Google’s SRE guidance describes this exact kind of cascading failure: retries can turn a relatively small overload into a much larger one. If each layer decides independently that a timeout is worth retrying, the original user action can multiply into a surprisingly large number of downstream attempts. That’s why I’m usually more suspicious of the retry topology than of one badly configured frontend. title: Day 9 of Building Crowdwide — I Almost Let It Sleep for 8-10 Days 💀
summary:
Puneet-Kumar2010 Posted on Oct 11 Day 9 of Building Crowdwide — I Almost Let It Sleep for 8-10 Days 💀 # discuss # buildinpublic # opensource # webdev So today is day 9 of building Crowdwide?? I don't feel like I'm going to write any code today. All features are done, all are working good! UI polishing also done, moderation done, suggestions implemented, reviews checked, all good! So what will I do today? It's time to just manage things and see some resources that might be useful. So I was checking what I can do more, and I found nothing to do with frontend and backend. But but but... I checked the billing of Crowdwide!! It was on the free tier, so it was just going to run out. But I didn't want Crowdwide to die!! So... I got another idea... I suspended Crowdwide on Render from one of my accounts, which had already used 560+ hours out of 750 hours (I created that account for projects I'm going to publish in public). AT THIS MOMENT I THOUGHT CROWDWIDE WAS GOING TO SLEEP FOR 8-10 DAYS THIS MONTH... BUT I'M A CRUEL DEVELOPER SO... I deployed Crowdwide from another account, which I use for my personal projects, and that one had only used 250+ hours out of 750. SO THAT PROBLEM IS SORTED, DEVS!! Then I tested all features on that new server and YAHH!! IT WAS WORKINGGGG!! And I had to do this because this project is built with 0 budget, no earnings, and I'm under 18, so no funding or investment. And again, I checked my admin console. No notifications there. Actually, it feels pretty easy to sort everything out now... because while developing, I tried to make it so that any action by a moderator had to be approved by the admin. Like, EVERY action. Moderators had to get approval just to review a post... and that was my FAAAAAAAAAAAAH system. So after getting reported about it by Harun (Moderator), I changed things as per his suggestions, and it feels so smooth now. Ohhh, I forgot to share the progress also! 10 members 37 posts shared 4 communities It feels slower than the past few days, ik it's just the 9th day of the V1 release, but still, in the initial days, it was feeling like it was growing faster. And I noticed the behaviour of users. They're creating accounts, engaging with some posts, liking and commenting mostly... THEN JUST OFF. They don't wanna post!! They don't wanna join communities!! DEAR USERS, SAY SOMETHING ALSO!! And one reality check is also there: there are 4 communities on Crowdwide, but only 2 are getting consistent posts at this stage, and those are also by me!! OHHHHHH USERS!!! YOU ALSO POST AND SAY SOMETHING!! A platform feels alive with 100-200 active users, not with 250 crore passive audience! But Crowdwide has 10 users only... 🙄 I think I roasted myself. But it's alright! And today is Sunday, and all the users who joined Crowdwide will receive a newsletter!! I'm waiting for it tbh. I know the timing, so I'll check it at that time (to see if the algorithm is giving good post suggestions or picking up the proper user's interests or not). Hmmm... and Crowdwide's new version... Crowdwide V2's release date will be announced soon 😂😅 🌐 Try Crowdwide: https://www.crowdwide.run.place 💻 GitHub: https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide That's all. How do you find Crowdwide? and Coinbase Analytics Challenge Readers share hackathon plans and career debates TL;DR Welcome back to Dev Opportunity Radar . This is a weekly series where I share opportunities, resources, communities, and interesting finds that I come across, with the goal of helping people discover things they might otherwise miss. This week's edition features the PayPal AI Hackathon , ARC Prize 2026 , and Coinbase's Strategy, Execution & Analytics Bounty Challenge , along with Build Your Own X as a resource for learning how different technologies work by building them from scratch. If you're new to the series, you can also browse previous editions, search past opportunities, and explore Community Finds , Reader Updates , and Resources Worth Checking Out on the Dev Opportunity Radar website . I've also written a short post about why I built it. You'll find links to both at the end of this article. If you've discovered something through the Radar, I'd love to hear about it. Whether you applied to an opportunity, joined a community, completed a program, or found a resource you hadn't seen before, I'd be happy to feature your experience in a future 💙 Reader Updates section (with your permission). And if you've come across an opportunity, resource, community, program, or event that deserves more attention, feel free to share it in the comments. If I feature one of your Community Finds in a future edition, I'll always make sure to credit you. If you discovered it, that recognition belongs to you. However, deadlines, eligibility, program details, and application requirements can change after publication. Before applying, please visit the official program page, review the latest information, and confirm that you're eligible. 🔄 Still Open From Previous Editions Before we get into this week's opportunities, here are a few from the two most recent editions that are still accepting applications. As the Radar has grown, there are now quite a few opportunities spread across the different editions. I used to keep all the still-open opportunities here, but I don't think repeating a long list every week makes the editions easier to read. So I keep this section to the two most recent editions as a quick reminder of opportunities you may have missed. Older opportunities are still available on the Dev Opportunity Radar website , where you can browse the full collection and use the filters to find something specific. I've already covered the opportunities below in detail, so I won't repeat everything here. If any of them catch your attention, you can go back to the original edition for the full overview, eligibility details, and application links. Opportunity Organization Type Format Deadline Featured In Nebius x NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon Nebius × NVIDIA Hackathon Online October 30 Edition #18 Pear Prime 2027 Pear Early-Career Program Hybrid January 4, 2027 Edition #19 Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB AI Hackathon Online October 18 Edition #19 Hacktoberfest 2026 MLH × DEV Open Source Event Online + In-person October 2026 Edition #19 📍 This Week's Opportunities Here are a few opportunities I came across this week that I thought were worth sharing. 📌 PayPal AI Hackathon Who it's for: Developers, designers, founders, students, and anyone interested in building with AI and payment technologies. What it's about: The PayPal AI Hackathon is a global online hackathon where participants build an application that meaningfully integrates PayPal's developer platform and an AI tool, model, or platform of their choice. There are no fixed problem statements or required tracks. Projects can include AI agents, payment experiences, business tools, applications, or automations. Participants can work individually or in teams, and they can start a new project or make meaningful progress on an existing one during the hackathon. A working prototype or proof of concept is required. Submissions must include a public code repository with a license, documentation, a functional demo, details of the AI tools used, and a demo video under three minutes. Static mockups and non-functional demos do not meet the requirements. The total prize pool is listed as $67,500+ , with awards for the overall winners and categories such as creativity, impact, agentic commerce, and the use of PayPal and sponsor tools. Some awards include cash, while others offer credits or subscriptions. Format: Online, worldwide Dates: Deadline November 13, 2026, at 1:30 AM IST Team Size: Individual or team Prize Pool: $67,500+ in cash and other prizes Requirement: Meaningful use of both PayPal and AI Explore the hackathon 📌 ARC Prize 2026 Who it's for: AI researchers, developers, and anyone interested in reasoning systems, AI agents, and open-source AI research. What it's about: ARC Prize 2026 is a competition focused on advancing AI reasoning, with $2 million in total prizes across three tracks . Participants can work on static reasoning tasks, interactive AI agents, or research papers exploring approaches to improving performance on the ARC-AGI benchmark. There are three tracks: ARC-AGI-2: Build systems that solve static reasoning tasks by predicting the correct outputs for visual grid-based problems. ARC-AGI-3: Build AI agents that explore unfamiliar environments, learn how they work, set goals, and plan actions without being given explicit instructions. Paper Prize: Submit a research paper presenting an approach to improving ARC-AGI performance, supported by a corresponding Kaggle code submission. The prize pools differ by track. ARC-AGI-2 has $700,000 available, ARC-AGI-3 has $850,000, and the Paper Prize has $450,000. Awards include prizes for high-scoring solutions, research contributions, and progress toward specific benchmarks. One important requirement is that participants must open-source their solutions to be eligible for prizes. Submissions are made through the designated Kaggle competitions, and internet access is unavailable during evaluation, so API-based systems such as GPT or Claude cannot be used during that stage. Format: Online, through Kaggle Competition Start: March 25, 2026 Submission Deadline: November 2, 2026 Paper Deadline: November 8, 2026 Results: December 4, 2026 Total Prize Pool: $2 million across three tracks Requirement: Reproducible, open-source solutions for prize eligibility Explore the competition Track details: ARC-AGI-2 ARC-AGI-3 Paper Prize 📌 Coinbase Strategy, Execution and Analytics Bounty Challenge Who it's for: People interested in analytics engineering, data modeling, SQL, Python, and data quality. What it's about: Coinbase's Strategy, Execution & Analytics team is running a bounty challenge built around a fictional scenario involving an Analytics Engineer intern supporting the Growth team. Participants must complete four exercises covering data modeling for an onboarding funnel, investigating inconsistencies across signup reports using Python, reviewing an inherited SQL pipeline, and communicating a metric discrepancy to a product manager. The challenge focuses on technical skills as well as decision-making, data validation, and explaining data issues to stakeholders. No live dataset is provided, so participants are expected to explain their assumptions and describe their solutions using code, schemas, or written responses where appropriate. Submissions must include a current resume in PDF format, responses to all four exercises within a combined limit of 1,500 words (excluding code blocks), and a brief disclosure explaining how AI tools were used, if applicable. The top 20 participants are eligible to receive $250 in USDC and an exploratory call with a Coinbase Emerging Talent recruiter. Participation does not count as a job application or guarantee an interview or internship. Format: Online bounty challenge Challenge Window: September 25 to October 18, 2026 Deadline: October 18, 2026, at 11:59 PM Pacific Time Prize: $250 in USDC per selected participant, plus a recruiter call Number of Recipients: 20 Eligibility: Legal residents of the United States or Canada, excluding Quebec, aged 18 or older, with a verified Coinbase account Challenge details and submission 📚 Resources Worth Checking Out Not every useful find comes with an application deadline. Here's one resource worth checking out this week. Build Your Own X Who it's for: Developers and learners who want to understand how programming concepts, tools, and technologies work by building them from scratch. What it's about: Build Your Own X is a GitHub repository maintained by CodeCrafters that collects step-by-step tutorials for recreating different technologies. Topics include databases, neural networks, programming languages, operating systems, web servers, Git, Docker, AI models, and more. The repository links to tutorials in different programming languages, covering projects ranging from building a simple neural network to implementing a database or creating a programming language. Readers can browse the categories and choose a project based on what they want to learn. It's a collection of external tutorials rather than a single structured course, so the languages, prerequisites, and difficulty levels vary between projects. Format: Free, open-source collection of tutorials Topics: Software Engineering, Systems Programming, AI/ML, Databases, Networking, and more Languages: Varies by tutorial Cost: Free Explore the repository 🌟 Community Finds One of my favorite things about this series has been seeing people share opportunities, communities, and resources that others might not have discovered otherwise. We've had some really wonderful community finds over the last few weeks, and I honestly can't thank everyone enough for taking the time to find these opportunities, look through them, and send them my way. I know that takes time, and I appreciate every person who thinks of the Radar when they come across something they feel others might find useful 💙 This week, we weren't able to include a community find, but that's completely okay. Hopefully we'll have more wonderful finds from the community as we keep going. So if you come across an opportunity, fellowship, grant, hackathon, conference, community, resource, or anything else you think more people should know about, please do send it my way. I love seeing what you find, and it helps make this series better for everyone. If I feature something you shared in a future edition, I'll always make sure to credit you. If you discovered it, that recognition belongs to you. One small request: If you're sharing an opportunity, please avoid posting raw URLs directly in the comments. DEV sometimes filters them before I get a chance to see them. A short description alongside the link makes it much easier for me to review and potentially feature it in a future edition. 💙 Reader Updates I'm looking forward to this section gradually growing over time, and I'd still love to hear from you. One of my favorite parts of writing Dev Opportunity Radar has been hearing from people who discovered something they otherwise might have missed. If you discovered an opportunity through the radar, applied to something, joined a community, attended an event, or simply found a resource you hadn't seen before, I'd genuinely love to hear about it. You don't need to have been accepted or have a big success story to share. Sometimes simply discovering the right opportunity at the right time is already a win. If you'd like to share an update, feel free to leave a comment on this edition. With your permission, I may feature it in a future 💙 Reader Updates section and tag you so other readers can celebrate your journey too. I hope this section gradually becomes a place where we can celebrate those stories together, one update at a time. 👋 Until Next Friday Before I go, I just want to say thank you. Every week, I spend time searching for opportunities, resources, and communities that I think deserve a little more attention. But one of my favorite parts of this series isn't the research. It's seeing what happens after an edition is published. Seeing someone discover an opportunity, apply to a program, share a resource, suggest a Community Find, or come back to tell us what they learned reminds me why I started Dev Opportunity Radar in the first place. The goal has always been simple: Help people discover opportunities they otherwise might have missed. Thanks to all of you, it feels like we're doing exactly that. Whether you've been reading since the very first edition or this is your first time here, thank you for being part of the journey. Every comment, suggestion, and shared opportunity helps make this series better than I could build on my own. If you ever come across an opportunity, resource, event, community, or anything else you think deserves more attention, I'd love for you to share it in the comments. And if Dev Opportunity Radar helped you discover something exciting, I'd love to hear that too. Thank you for reading, for sharing, and for helping make this our radar , not just mine. Jem for The DEV Team Posted on Sep 23 • Edited on Sep 28 • AI-assisted Join the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge: $2,500 in Prizes for FIVE Winners! # devchallenge # machinelearning # ai # kagglechallenge Open-ended scope for custom model testing We're excited to team up with Kaggle for a brand new challenge! Running through October 11 , the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge asks you to build a benchmark, run it against real models, and tell us what you found. Today's models reason, write code, use tools, and hold multi-turn conversations, and their capabilities will likely change by tomorrow. Public leaderboards only tell you so much, so why not test them against the work you actually do? Kaggle Benchmarks lets you build your own evaluations and run them across a suite of models to see how they really stack up. So pick something you've always wondered about, measure it, and show your work. There's a $2,500 prize pool up for grabs across five winners! Read on to learn more. Our Prompt Build a Benchmark Your mandate is to build a benchmark on Kaggle and write about what you learned. Your post should cover: What task(s) did you run? Prizes 🏆 Five winners will each receive: $500 USD cash prize DEV++ Membership Exclusive DEV Badge All participants with a valid submission will receive a completion badge on their DEV profile. title: FarbeDex: a colour picker that only works outside (and never needs the internet)
summary: Subarna Maity Posted on Oct 11 FarbeDex: a colour picker that only works outside (and never needs the internet) # hf26challenge # devchallenge # gemma # android Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Submission 🌿 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built I pick colours for a living, and almost all of them come from other screens: palette generators, screenshots, a hex code a client pasted into chat. Meanwhile the best palettes I've ever seen were outside my window the whole time. Moss on a wet wall. A late sky fading from peach to blue. Rust on a gate nobody has painted in years. So I built FarbeDex , an Android app that turns what you see outside into colours you can keep. It takes almost no time. Point your camera at the view, the sky, a cloud, even the clouds below you from a plane window, and tap once. The palette appears right away, with how much of the scene each colour covers. Pick your two favourites, Gemma names them a moment later, and your phone goes back in your pocket. You go back to the view. Your favourites join a collection of 151 colours, from everyday greys to Mythical vivid violets, each one a little colour pal with its own face. And every catch hands you a palette you can drop straight into your next design. Most apps that get you outside give you a job: run this far, find this bird, finish this quest. FarbeDex gives you none. No checklist, no target, no streak. When something makes you stop and look, that's your catch. And it all runs completely offline , with two open AI models living on your phone. Demo Home: your collection at a glance Catch, then pick your two favourites A Legendary reveal Your FarbeDex fills up Gemma naming colours in airplane mode 🎬 Demo video: 📱 APK: https://github.com/Dronzer2code/FarbeDex/releases/tag/v4.0 Code Dronzer2code / FarbeDex FarbeDex Catch real colours from real places. FarbeDex is an offline Android app for designers and front-end developers. You go outside, photograph a scene with the in-app camera, and FarbeDex extracts its palette and how much of the scene each colour covers. Every colour lands in the FarbeDex: a fixed index of 151 colour entries (#001–#151) that you complete over time. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass. Screenshots and demo video: TODO (added after the field test) APK download: TODO (GitHub release v1.0.0) How it works Camera only. There is no way to import a picture. Live checks (hand-held motion, a fresh capture) and the Referee make sure a catch is a real outdoor scene, not a screen or a print. Deterministic colour maths. The photo is reduced to up to 7 colours with k-means in OKLab, and each colour's share of the scene… View on GitHub How I Built It The maths sees, the models judge and name The biggest decision was what not to give to AI. Colour extraction is plain maths: k-means clustering in OKLab, a colour space built around how people perceive difference. The same photo always gives the same palette. Every colour lands in one of 151 entries: 7 neutrals plus 16 hue families × 3 lightness × 3 chroma bands. I wanted the collection to be completable, so a test sweeps the whole sRGB cube and checks that all 151 entries can actually be reached. Rarity follows one idea, "how often does nature show this colour": greens and greys are everywhere, vivid blues and violets are not. That gives 42 Common, 42 Uncommon, 37 Rare, 21 Legendary and 9 Mythical. The models do only what models are good at: judging a scene, and naming things. Gemma 3 270M, the namer that fits in your pocket The star of FarbeDex is Gemma 3 270M , running on the phone through llama.cpp as a 253 MB file. When you register colours, Gemma names each new one, gives the whole palette a one-word mood (COOL, EARTHY, SERENE…), and writes a one-line tip on using the palette in an interface. A 270M model has big ideas and small habits, so it never writes free text into the app: Structured output only. Every request uses a JSON schema compiled into a grammar, and the schema pins exactly which colours Gemma must name. It can't skip one or invent one. Gemma writes the poetry, the app writes the facts. Early on, Gemma named a pale blue "Dark Charcoal". Now Gemma writes only the evocative part ("Rooftop Morning"), and the app adds the true colour word ("…Blue"). Colour words are banned from Gemma's half, so a blue is always called blue. Validate, retry once, then fall back. Every name is checked for length, uniqueness and a blocklist. A failed name gets one retry with the reason attached; after that a plain name like "Vivid Pale Blue" takes over, so you're never left waiting. My first Legendary indigo came back as Ocean Waves . Here it is in the Tailwind export, next to the plain fallback names of colours Gemma hadn't named yet: More names Gemma gave my catches: [2–4 more names from your catches] MobileCLIP, the referee that keeps it honest The second open model is MobileCLIP-S0 on ONNX Runtime. It answers two questions: is this a real outdoor scene, and what's in it? The phone never runs a text encoder. I embedded every label on my laptop ("a computer monitor", "potted plants on a balcony", "the blue sky"…) and ship them as a small file, so on the phone one image embedding and a few dot products do the job. It rejects only confident screens and home interiors, so balconies, rooftops and pot plants all count. And the subject it names must match the photo's real colours. Yes, I tried to cheat by photographing my own laptop. It didn't work: Pick two, and sometimes get lucky Catching shouldn't be mindless, so you choose two favourites per catch, and only those join your collection. Rare, Legendary and Mythical picks get a special reveal, and each has a 1-in-400 chance to be shiny : gold rim, sparkles and its own chiptune jingle, all original and generated in code. Two AI teammates, one source of truth I built FarbeDex in about two and a half days with two AI tools, each with its own job. GitHub Copilot is the editor. While Claude builds, Copilot keeps the documentation updated in parallel, so the docs never fall behind the code. When each Claude task finishes, Copilot curates the commit message, turning a long session into one clean line of history. Specs go in; tested, documented commits come out. The repo ships with 279 passing tests. We Touched Grass I'm a graphic designer and a front-end developer, which mostly means I'm a person at a desk. My whole working day happens on a laptop. When the work stops, the scrolling starts: my "free time" was Instagram Reels until my thumb got tired. I didn't notice what it was doing to me until it had already done it. I went out less, talked to people less, and slowly got bad at simple things: starting a conversation, being somewhere without a screen, just being outside. Climbing back out took real, slow work, and I did most of it alone. Nobody hands you a plan for that. So I know exactly where the problem sits. People like me know the outdoors exists. What we lack is a reason to step out that doesn't come with pressure. Every reason the internet offers is another task: 10,000 steps, a streak, a specific bird. When you're already drained, one more task is exactly what keeps you at your desk. FarbeDex is built for that version of me. For a designer, colour is the reason. There's no target and no wrong answer. You walk to the corner, notice the light on a wall, and tap once. That moment becomes something real for your work, and a little colour pal you actually want to show people. Everything runs on the phone, so you can leave the Wi-Fi, and the feed, behind. Then comes the moment later, back at the desk. You remember that evening and think: those colours were so good, I wish I had them in my design. Now you do, in five formats: Palette image : a swatch card with a one-word mood, ready for a moodboard. HEX codes : copy any colour with one tap. CSS : custom properties to paste into a stylesheet. Tailwind : a colors block for your config. JSON : design tokens for Figma plugins and design systems. A built-in contrast table even tells you which pairs pass WCAG for text, so the sky you saw can become a readable website. Here's what happened when I used it myself: [Your first walks with FarbeDex: balcony, roof, the street near home. How long you stayed out, how many colours you caught, your rarest find, a shiny if you got one, and what it felt like to look up instead of down. 2–3 photos.] [Your FarbeDex counter before and after, e.g. "0 / 151 → 2 / 151".] Why Does Open Innovation Matter? It works where colour lives. Parks, rooftops and planes often have no signal. Both models (276 MB together) run fully on the phone, in airplane mode. Your photos stay yours. Nothing is uploaded, there's no account, and the only permission FarbeDex asks for is the camera. It costs nothing per catch. No API bill, no rate limit, and it will work exactly the same next year. You can see inside it. Every prompt, label and threshold is in the repo. Don't like the names? Change the prompt. Want a different referee? It's one config line. A big closed vision model might label scenes a little better. But it would need every outdoor photo uploaded, a signal in the middle of a park, and money for each catch. For noticing colours on a walk, two tiny open models are exactly enough. What Didn't Work The quantized referee saw screens everywhere. The int8 version of MobileCLIP called a beach, a lake and a savanna "a screen". Switching to the fp16 file (23 MB) fixed it completely. My own balcony counted as indoors. On the phone, every shot from my balcony and roof was rejected as "inside". I flipped the logic: accept by default, and reject only when the model is sure it sees a screen or a home interior. A sky called "fern". One prompt per subject wasn't enough. Several prompts per subject, plus a rule that the label must match the photo's real colours, fixed it. No green, no fern. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma : Gemma 3 270M runs fully offline on an Android phone, naming colours, giving palettes a mood and writing design tips through validated, schema-constrained JSON. Team Subarna Maity - Me *Sourish Panda - @t-rexbytes * I set out to build a colour picker that makes you go outside. What I ended up with is an app that, most days, just asks you to look up. 🌿 Top comments (0) Subscribe Personal Trusted User Create template Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. title: I Built an AI Gardening App That Tells Me to Put the Laptop Down
summary:
Shubhra Pokhariya Posted on Oct 11 • AI-assisted I Built an AI Gardening App That Tells Me to Put the Laptop Down # devchallenge # hf26challenge # showdev # gemma Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Submission 🌿 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Coding is my thing. Gardening is a part of who I am. I have hundreds of pots, and I know my plants through the little things they show me. I notice which ones respond well to buried banana peels, which seem happier with used tea granules or old buttermilk, and which need my lunch-box system instead of raw kitchen scraps buried around them. I watch their leaves, new growth and flowers. I do not need an app to tell me how to care for my own plants. That understanding comes from spending time with them. But it made me think about how a tool could help someone who is still learning to notice these things. For a long time coding and gardening lived in different corners of my day. I would code for hours, then walk away from the screen to be with my plants, and the two never really met. This challenge gave me a reason to put them in the same room. So first, thank you to the DEV team and everyone behind it. You gave me the opportunity to write code about the thing I love most, and I enjoyed every hour of it. The question I almost asked an AI On 30 September I moved my marigold out of a shady, bright corner and into the open sun. The corner was there to keep the heavy rain off it. It grew from a cutting of a plant that came up by itself from last year's seeds, so it already feels a little like family. On 5 October I counted about three open flowers and three buds. On 9 October I counted seven open flowers and five buds. My first thought was to ask an AI why. An answer would have been easy to get and easy to believe. But the sun, rain and time passing had all played a part, and I couldn't tell which one made the difference. Neither could an AI. So I asked a different question. Not "why is my plant doing this?" but "what should I look at before I change anything?" That question became Garden Trials. What I Built Garden Trials is a small app that runs entirely on your own computer. The whole idea fits in one line, which is look first, change one thing, let the garden answer. I do not like screens near my plants. When I am with them I want my hands in the soil and my phone away. Sometimes a bloom looks so good that I click a photo, for myself and for other plant lovers. So I built the app the way I wish gardening tools worked. It talks to me before and after, and in the middle it asks me to put the laptop down and go and look. I write a note about a plant and the day I saw it. A local Gemma model reads it into plain facts. The app asks me to check one specific thing on the plant. Until I write down what I found, it will not suggest anything. I either watch, or pick one change from a small fixed menu, ideally leaving a similar plant alone to compare. I count and take a photo. The app shows me the last photo so I can match the angle. I get a table, a chart, a verdict, an evidence level from 0 to 3, and one plain next step. It is not a plant doctor. It never says what is wrong with a plant, and it never says what caused a result. Garden Trials is for gardeners who are still learning to read their plants, and for anyone who wants to check their assumptions rather than jump to conclusions. It brings observations, follow-up checks, simple experiments and evidence tracking into one process. Instead of just recording what happened, it helps gardeners look at what changed, what else might have affected the result, and what their observations can actually tell them. It is not meant to replace the understanding that grows from spending time with plants, but to encourage closer observation. Demo The quickest way in is the sample garden. Tick "Try the illustrative sample garden" in the sidebar and you can walk through the whole loop with made-up plants. Nothing from it is ever saved to a real garden. Code shubhrapokhariya / garden-trials Local Gemma 3 1B app (Ollama + Streamlit) that sends gardeners back to their plants to look first, helps them test one change at a time, and assigns each result an evidence level from 0 to 3. 🌱 Garden Trials Look first. Change one thing. Let the garden answer. A small local app for gardeners. A Gemma model running on your own laptop helps you write down what you
see and asks one thing to go and check on the plant. Plain Python builds the experiment, keeps the
records and works out how much the evidence really shows. The app never says what caused a result. Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass. Demo video (48 seconds, no sound): https://youtu.be/Rm7X4btlZVk Quickstart Install Python 3.11 or newer and Ollama . The tests were run on Python 3.11. Download the code, then in its folder run: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
ollama pull gemma3:1b
python -m streamlit run app.py Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode On Windows you can double-click run.bat instead. On macOS or Linux, run bash run.sh . Both scripts
still start the app if Ollama is missing… View on GitHub Setup is in the README: Python 3.11 or newer, Ollama, ollama pull gemma3:1b , then python -m streamlit run app.py . The folder examples/my-garden/ holds my real notes, counts and photos from this week. Start the app with GARDEN_DIR=examples/my-garden and you can read them without touching your own data. My real garden, this week Petunia On 7 October I counted two open flowers, one spent flower, four buds and a lot of tiny buds forming. I took photos and counts on 7, 8, 9 and 10 October, but I only opened the app on the 10th, so I typed the first three days in afterwards. The app marks those entries as backfilled, which is exactly what they are. It is also why the trial says it started on 10 October. When I saved the 7 October note, Gemma's reading dropped a number, so the app threw the reading away and kept my words exactly as I wrote them. Then Gemma's Look First question turned out to be about pests or disease, which I had never mentioned. The app blocked it and asked its own question instead: Count the open flowers and the buds right now. Do the newest shoots have buds? I went and looked on the 10th. Four open flowers, two bright ones on top and two darker ones lower down that had just opened, and small buds at the tips of the shoots. Date Open flowers Buds Note 7 Oct 2 4 Front view. One spent flower not counted. 8 Oct 2 4 Removed the spent flower. Photo from above. 9 Oct 2 4 Buds clearly bigger and longer. 10 Oct 4 2 Two buds opened. Bright sun, so the reds look brighter. I removed one spent flower on the 8th. That was routine upkeep, not a test, but I want to say so. There was no comparison plant, and petunia buds open on their own anyway. The app gave this evidence level 0 and said it plainly. No change was made during these counts, so it shows what the plant did while I watched and says nothing about a cause. The two new flowers opened darker and more velvety than the older ones. I read that a new petal is still small and tightly folded, so its colour is packed close together, and that as the flower opens fully and stretches out, the same colour spreads over a bigger petal and looks lighter. So I guess that is what I am seeing. Marigold The 5 October photo was taken for myself, not for the trial. I clicked it just because the plant looked lovely, from the side, and only later decided to use it here. One bud is partly cut off at the edge. The 9 October photo is the one I took for the trial, from above, where every flower and bud can be seen. My first count may have missed buds I could not see from the side, so the jump from 3 to 7 open flowers is in my notes, but it is not a fair comparison. A few petals also looked flattened after some rain. The rain may be the reason, but that is a guess. Bougainvillea Five cuttings, about a month and a half old, in the same soil and the same small black nursery bags on the same bench. One of them already has two pink flowers and the other four have none. Its mother plant is in full bloom, while my other bougainvilleas are only starting. My guess, not tested, is the variety or the time of year. The cuttings are different varieties, so "same soil, same bench" is not a fair test. A real test needs cuttings of the same variety, taken at the same time from different mother plants. How I Built It The stack is small on purpose: Streamlit , one JSON file, and gemma3:1b running locally through Ollama . I picked the 1B Gemma model to find out whether this idea works on an ordinary laptop with no cloud account. On a laptop CPU an answer can take up to a minute. Gemma has three jobs. It reads my note into plain facts, suggests one thing to go and check, and picks one change from a short menu. Everything that has to be reliable lives in plain Python, because I treat the model's output the way I would treat any untrusted input. If a number from my note is missing in Gemma's reading, the reading is rejected and my exact words are kept. Details Gemma adds that I did not write are removed by a word-match check. It is a loose check, so it can miss some. The cause field is forced to "unknown" in code. Pest and disease questions are blocked unless I raised them first. Trials come from a fixed menu that is filtered per plant. "Water more" is never offered for bougainvillea, which likes to stay on the dry side. Verdicts and evidence levels are calculated by code, never by Gemma. Level 3 needs two finished trials of the same change, each with a comparison plant and nothing else changed, all pointing the same way. Saves go to a temporary file first and are then swapped in. A garden file that cannot be read is moved aside and never overwritten. The tests replace Gemma with fake and deliberately bad answers, such as garbage, dropped numbers, invented pests, off-menu picks. A second set drives the real pages end to end. There are 85 tests, and none of them needs Ollama. What went wrong The model did not behave in my own garden. Gemma's reading of all three of my notes was rejected by the number check, and one of its three questions was blocked. The other two questions got through, and they were generic. "Is the plant's stem straight?" had nothing to do with what I was seeing, so I wrote down what I actually noticed. The guards block invented pests. They cannot make a small model's question a good one. They also only catch the failures I thought of, and the checks match English words, so notes in Hindi are not checked the same way. In my real garden Gemma only read my notes and wrote Look First questions. Both of my real trials were watch-only, so it never picked a trial there. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Gemma runs on my laptop through Ollama. There is no API key, no usage bill and no cloud AI call. My notes and photos sit in a folder on my own machine, and the photos are saved without their location data. Setup needs the internet once, to download the packages, Ollama and the model, and I switched off Streamlit's anonymous usage statistics. Running Gemma locally let me build and test this idea without an API key and without paying for every request. I could try it as often as I liked, and if a better small model arrives, I change one setting ( OLLAMA_MODEL ) and the rest of the app stays as it is. The small model had clear limitations, which I describe above, but that was part of what I wanted to learn, which is how far an open model can take this idea on an ordinary laptop, with ordinary code checking its output. The experiment showed me both the value of running a model locally and the limits of relying on its answers. What I took away The point of the app is what happens when I close the laptop. It asks me to go and look, and I stand there with the plant and nothing else. It cannot tell whether I really went outside, and I will not pretend it can. That pause is a promise I make to myself. The AI can suggest what to look at. The garden gives the answer. Thank you for reading, and thank you again to the DEV team for a challenge that let me bring the two things I love together.
